title: Lessons from Lloyd Cantrell and the Imperial method book
summary: He took lessons from Cantrell using the Imperial method book, and can read anything, including heavy overtures with Pritchett's band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Oh, 1914. And you remember any of the drummers when you were a boy that you used to like, that you'd listen to, or follow around on parades, or any other places you'd hear them?
Lloyd Cantrell. That's where I took lessons from him. He got a son. He got a son, but his son was a baby.
Lloyd, Lloyd. He played clandette now, yeah. His dad took lessons, yeah. Lloyd was small, yeah.
You played with Jim Robinson and Ernie Cagnolotti last night.
Did you start right in with the lessons with Mr. Cantrell?
Do you remember anything about how he taught you, or what kind of a book he used? Oh, yeah. Did he use a book for you right away, or? Right away.
Imperial method book. Mm-hmm. I've seen those for some instruments. I never did see it for drums. Do you happen to have any of that old music you started with? Did you ever save that?
I've been learning my grandkids. I can read anything with drums. I'm going to have some parts here.
I just wondered if you ever saved that old imperial book.

Oh, it's got a new method now. My grandkids got the book, I wanted to leave it here by his house he got it. I played with Pritchard Band, them heavy overtures, yeah. I read anything. See, before I was back with the swing, I used to like to read, played them reading all you see. Yeah, you see. After I found out Jazz had it, that's the best.
